Retirement is a big milestone, and it's important to prepare yourself financially for that stage of life. Part of that means learning about Social Security and understanding how the program works. A key part of Social Security is the fact that benefits are eligible for a cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, every year. The purpose of those COLAs is to help benefits keep up with inflation. But there are many things about COLAs that seniors on Social Security don't know, and not knowing these four facts could make it harder to plan financially for the future. Read More Here › SPONSORED COLAs are not based on senior-specific expenses Since COLAs are meant to help Social Security benefits keep up with inflation , you'd think they'd be based on senior-specific expenses. But that's not the case. Social Security COLAs are based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which tracks the spending patterns of working Americans. Advocates have pushed for lawmakers to change the Social Security COLA formula to be based on a senior-specific index, since retirees tend to spend differently than people who work. Such an index already exists, and it's known as the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E). But lawmakers have hesitated to adopt this change because the CPI-E is considered experimental by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, among other reasons. Because COLAs don't tend to accurately reflect the costs seniors face, Social Security benefits have been losing buying power. The Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group, says Social Security recipients have lost 13.7% of their buying power over the past 10 years. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. COLAs are based on third-quarter data Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) isn't based on inflation predictions. It's calculated using actual inflation data from the third quarter of the year. To calculate the adjustment, the SSA looks at the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). Specifically, it compares the average CPI-W for July, August, and September with the average for the third quarter of the last year a COLA took effect. If the index has increased, beneficiaries receive a corresponding adjustment, rounded to the nearest tenth of a percentage point. The Social Security Administration (SSA) has already announced a 3.6% COLA for 2027. The increase will apply to Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits beginning in January 2027. But retirees who are already thinking about their 2028 benefits may be interested in what's coming next. The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) issued its first estimate for the 2028 COLA in November 2026, projecting another 3.6% increase. For comparison, the Social Security Administration's 2026 Trustees Report projects a 2.4% COLA for 2028 under its intermediate assumptions. These figures are projections, not guarantees, and the actual adjustment will depend on inflation data collected during the third quarter of 2027. The SSA typically announces the following year's COLA in October, after the September inflation data becomes available. Until then, any 2028 figure should be treated as an estimate rather than a promise of how much benefits will increase. There's no such thing as a negative COLA When there's a rise in the CPI-W during the third quarter of the year compared to the previous year, Social Security benefits are eligible for an increase. When there's no rise in the CPI-W year over year, benefits remain flat. But the same thing also happens when the CPI-W decreases from year to year. Social Security benefits can't decrease from one year to the next, even if prices decline. Learn More Here › SPONSORED COLAs can be wiped out by Medicare Part B increases People enrolled in Social Security and Medicare at the same time have their monthly Part B premiums, which cover outpatient care, deducted from their benefits automatically.  This means that if there's a large increase in the cost of  Medicare Part B  and only a small COLA, that raise can be effectively  wiped out. For example, let's say the average monthly Social Security benefit is $2,100 and it gets only a 1% COLA. That leads to an increase of $21. But if the cost of Medicare Part B also rises by $21, seniors could be left with no net raise whatsoever. It's also possible for the cost of Medicare Part B to increase enough year over year that it exceeds a given COLA. In the example above, if there was a $22 increase in the cost of Medicare Part B, it would outpace the COLA for the average benefit. The good news is that seniors cannot see their Social Security benefits reduced from one year to the next because of a Medicare Part B cost increase. Thanks to what's known as the hold harmless provision, in a situation like that, benefits would stay the same. They wouldn't decrease. Bottom line Without COLAs, Social Security recipients would be pretty much guaranteed to lose buying power over time. So the fact that COLAs exist is a very good thing, despite some flaws in the way they're calculated. But understanding how COLAs work could help you eliminate some stress living on Social Security . That means knowing what they can and cannot do. While Social Security COLAs can help you keep up with inflation, they're not meant to help you get ahead of inflation. And if you don't make an effort to save well for retirement or have income outside of your monthly benefits, you may end up struggling to cover your bills. So it's important not to rely too heavily on COLAs, and to instead find ways to boost your senior income yourself.
